opus-5.5.text:
I think what struck me most is that it treats the model as a replaceable component rather than the center of the product. With Claude Code, the experience is very tightly co-designed with one model family. The tool prompts, the way it plans, how it reads files and recovers from errors are all tuned around how Claude behaves. That's a strength, because you get a very polished loop, but it also means the harness and the model are kind of married.

What OpenClaude showed is that if you build the harness in a more open way, you can route different parts of the task to different models. You might use a strong reasoning model for planning or for a hard debugging step, and a cheaper, faster model for routine edits, searching the codebase, or summarizing context. Users started mixing and matching, and they found that for many tasks the gap between models was smaller than people assumed, as long as the scaffolding was good.

For someone like me who works on models, that's both encouraging and humbling. It's encouraging because it means open models, including ours, can actually get used in real agentic workflows, not just benchmarks. It's humbling because it tells you that a lot of the perceived capability comes from the system around the model: how context is managed, how tools are described, how failures are handled. So you can't just optimize the model in isolation anymore. You have to think about how it behaves inside a harness it wasn't specifically designed for, whether it follows tool formats robustly, whether it stays coherent over long sessions, whether it knows when to stop.

And I think the multi-model approach points toward where things are going. Instead of one giant model doing everything, you'll have a kind of team, with different models playing different roles and the harness acting as the coordinator. That changes what "a good model" means. It's not only about peak intelligence. It's about being reliable, cost-efficient, and a good collaborator inside a larger system.

r001.rationale: The response discusses routing different task parts to different models and users mixing models, but it does not say OpenClaude autonomously selects a model for understanding a submitted video or removes that choice from the user.

fable-5.1.text:
What impressed me most was that OpenClaude doesn't treat the model as a single thing. In Claude Code, the whole experience is built around one frontier model doing almost everything, from planning to editing to summarizing. That's elegant, but it means you pay frontier prices and frontier latency for every step, even the trivial ones.

OpenClaude takes a different stance. It treats the model as a routing problem. The orchestration layer looks at each step and asks what level of capability this actually requires. Reading a file and deciding whether it's relevant? A small, fast model handles that. Generating a diff across several files with subtle dependencies? That goes to a strong model. Writing the final summary for the user? Something in between. So in a single task you might see three or four different models cooperating, and the user never has to think about it.

Two things stood out to me as genuinely clever. First, the cheap models aren't just doing cheap work. They're acting as filters that shrink the context before it ever reaches the expensive model. That compounds. Less noise in the context means the big model reasons better, not just cheaper. Second, OpenClaude lets you plug in open-weight models alongside commercial APIs. For a lot of teams in China, that's not a nice-to-have. That's the whole reason they can deploy it at all.

The honest trade-off is consistency. When one model does everything, it has a coherent memory of its own reasoning across the task. When you split the work, you introduce handoffs, and handoffs are where information gets lost. OpenClaude has done a lot of engineering to make those handoffs clean, but I don't think the problem is fully solved. Claude Code's single-model design is simpler and more predictable, and sometimes simple wins.

So my view is that these represent two bets. Claude Code bets that frontier models will keep getting cheaper and faster, so routing becomes unnecessary. OpenClaude bets that the gap between small and large models will persist long enough that intelligent allocation matters. I actually think both bets are partly right, and the interesting question is what the system looks like when you combine them.

r001.rationale: The response describes OpenClaude routing different coding-task steps to suitable models, but it does not mention submitted videos or selecting a model to understand one.

astra-6.text: What impressed me was the flexibility of using multiple models together. You don’t have to assume one model is best at every part of a coding task—you can give different parts to models with different strengths. Compared with Claude Code, that’s the aspect of OpenClaude I’d highlight: how the models work together, rather than just how capable any single model is.

sol-6.1.text: What impressed me was the flexibility. Claude Code is built around Claude, while OpenClaude treats different models as resources you can coordinate. You can choose a model based on the task—one for planning, another for implementation, another for review. The interesting part is how you divide the work and bring the results together.
